content: The test image shows a soybean stem split lengthwise with **white/cream pith** and **dark, rotted root tissue**. This is a critical diagnostic feature. Let me compare top candidates.

The Fusarium reference (bottom-right panel) shows very similar split-stem imagery with white pith and dark rotted roots — very close to the test image. Let me look more carefully at a few more to confirm.

**Analysis summary:**

- **Test image**: Mature soybean stem split lengthwise, showing **white/cream pith**, with **heavily rotted, dark/black root tissue** at the base. Green outdoor background. The stem interior has no brown discoloration.

**Key differential diagnosis:**
- **Sudden Death Syndrome (SDS)**: White pith (explicit diagnostic marker) + rotted taproots/lateral roots → **MATCHES**
- **Brown Stem Rot**: Brown pith — clearly does NOT match (pith is white)
- **Fusarium**: Brown vascular tissue in roots and stems — the vascular tissue in the test image appears pale/white, not brown
- **Charcoal Rot**: Should show black microsclerotia specks beneath epidermis → none visible
- **Phytophthora**: Chocolate-brown stem discoloration extending upward → not present; stem is white/pale
- **White Mold**: Fluffy white mycelium + black sclerotia → not present

The **white pith** is the single most critical diagnostic feature here. Per the knowledge base: *"SDS-infected plants have white pith when stems are cut, distinguishing it from brown stem rot which causes brown pith discoloration."* Combined with the heavily rotted, decomposed dark root system — this is a textbook SDS split-stem diagnostic presentation.
